claim: The lateral wall of the mouse subventricular zone harbors neural stem cells (NSC, B cells) which generate proliferating transient-amplifying progenitors (TAP, C cells) that ultimately give rise to neuroblasts (NB, A cells).
source: The lateral wall of the mouse subventricular zone harbors neural stem cells (NSC, B cells) which generate proliferating transient-amplifying progenitors (TAP, C cells) that ultimately give rise to neuroblasts (NB, A cells).
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the cellular organization of the SVZ, supported by the study's findings and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Molecular profiling at the single-cell level struggles to distinguish different cell types in the SVZ.
source: Molecular profiling at the single-cell level struggles to distinguish these different cell types.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and is supported by the authors' analysis comparing their sorted populations to published scRNAseq data.

claim: There exists an abundant, clonogenic and multipotent population of immature neuroblasts (iNB cells) at the transition between TAP and migrating NB (mNB).
source: Here, we combined transcriptome analyses of FACS-sorted cells and single-cell RNAseq to demonstrate the existence of an abundant, clonogenic and multipotent population of immature neuroblasts (iNB cells) at the transition between TAP and migrating NB (mNB).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through FACS sorting, transcriptome analysis, and functional assays.

claim: iNB cells are reversibly engaged in neuronal differentiation.
source: iNB are reversibly engaged in neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multipotency and plasticity data shown in the differentiation and transplantation experiments.

claim: iNB cells keep molecular features of both undifferentiated progenitors, plasticity and unexpected regenerative properties.
source: Indeed, they keep molecular features of both undifferentiated progenitors, plasticity and unexpected regenerative properties.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic data showing expression of both progenitor and neuroblast markers, and functional data showing multipotency.

claim: iNB cells undergo important progressive molecular switches, including changes in the expression of splicing regulators leading to their differentiation in mNB.
source: Strikingly, they undergo important progressive molecular switches, including changes in the expression of splicing regulators leading to their differentiation in mNB subdividing them into two subtypes, iNB1 and iNB2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microarray and scRNAseq data showing differential expression of RNA splicing regulators.

claim: iNB cells can be subdivided into two subtypes, iNB1 and iNB2.
source: Strikingly, they undergo important progressive molecular switches, including changes in the expression of splicing regulators leading to their differentiation in mNB subdividing them into two subtypes, iNB1 and iNB2.
evidence: This subdivision is based on Dcx expression levels and molecular profiling data.

claim: Due to their plastic properties, iNB could represent a new target for regenerative therapy of brain damage.
source: Due to their plastic properties, iNB could represent a new target for regenerative therapy of brain damage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the demonstrated plasticity and regenerative properties of iNB cells.

claim: The sub-granular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampus and the subventricular zone (SVZ) are two restricted neurogenic areas of the adult mammalian brain where new neurons are constantly produced from neural stem cells.
source: New neurons are constantly produced from neural stem cells (NSC) throughout life in two restricted neurogenic areas of the adult mammalian brain: the sub-granular zone (SGZ) of the hippocampus and the subventricular zone (SVZ; Obernier and Alvarez-Buylla, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The lateral wall (LW) of the SVZ, adjacent to the striatum, is the largest germinal zone of the adult mouse brain.
source: The lateral wall (LW) of the SVZ, adjacent to the striatum, is the largest germinal zone of the adult mouse brain, in which NSC (type B1 cells) are produced during the embryonic development and are mostly in a quiescent state thereafter (Codega et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NSC (type B1 cells) in the SVZ are produced during embryonic development and are mostly in a quiescent state thereafter.
source: The lateral wall (LW) of the SVZ, adjacent to the striatum, is the largest germinal zone of the adult mouse brain, in which NSC (type B1 cells) are produced during the embryonic development and are mostly in a quiescent state thereafter (Codega et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Upon activation, NSC divide and give rise to rapidly dividing transit-amplifying cells (TAP, type C cells), which ultimately produce neuroblasts (NB, type A cells).
source: Upon activation, NSC divide and give rise to rapidly dividing transit-amplifying cells (TAP, type C cells), which ultimately produce neuroblasts (NB, type A cells).
evidence: This describes the established lineage progression in the SVZ, which is well-known in the field.

claim: Neuroblasts migrate out of the SVZ anteriorly along blood vessels and the rostral migratory stream (RMS) to reach the olfactory bulb (OB) where they integrate and differentiate into various subtypes of interneurons required to fine-tune odor discrimination.
source: These neuroblasts migrate out of the SVZ anteriorly along blood vessels and the rostral migratory stream (RMS) to reach the olfactory bulb (OB) where they integrate and differentiate into various subtypes of interneurons required to fine-tune odor discrimination (Obernier and Alvarez-Buylla, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroblast migration and differentiation, supported by a citation.

claim: The diversity of the OB interneurons depends on the intrinsic regional identity of NSC in the SVZ along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes.
source: The diversity of the OB interneurons depends on the intrinsic regional identity of NSC in the SVZ along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes (Obernier and Alvarez-Buylla, 2019; Merkle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NSC and neural progenitors present in the SVZ are proficient to produce astrocytes and oligodendrocytes that migrate toward the corpus callosum, the RMS and the striatum in the normal adult brain.
source: Besides their neurogenic fate, NSC and neural progenitors present in the SVZ are also proficient to produce astrocytes and oligodendrocytes that migrate toward the corpus callosum, the RMS and the striatum in the normal (Gonzalez-Perez and Alvarez-Buylla, 2011; Hack et al., 2005; Sohn et al., 2015) and injured adult brain (Holmin et al., 1997; Nait-Oumesmar et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NSC and neural progenitors present in the SVZ are proficient to produce astrocytes and oligodendrocytes that migrate toward the corpus callosum, the RMS and the striatum in the injured adult brain.
source: Besides their neurogenic fate, NSC and neural progenitors present in the SVZ are also proficient to produce astrocytes and oligodendrocytes that migrate toward the corpus callosum, the RMS and the striatum in the normal (Gonzalez-Perez and Alvarez-Buylla, 2011; Hack et al., 2005; Sohn et al., 2015) and injured adult brain (Holmin et al., 1997; Nait-Oumesmar et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses using different combinations of cell surface markers and transgenic mice models to isolate SVZ cells have provided important initial insights into stem cell quiescence and have highlighted consecutive transitions during neuronal lineage progression.
source: Transcriptomic analyses using different combinations of cell surface markers and transgenic mice models to isolate SVZ cells have provided important initial insights into stem cell quiescence and have highlighted consecutive transitions during neuronal lineage progression (Codega et al., 2014; Belenguer et al., 2021; Fischer et al., 2011; Mich et al., 2014; Pastrana et al., 2009).
evidence: This summarizes previous work in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing has revolutionized the field and has made it possible to precisely elucidate the transcriptome of SVZ cells present in the LW.
source: Since then, the single-cell RNA-sequencing has revolutionized the field and has made it possible to precisely elucidate the transcriptome of SVZ cells present in the LW (Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021; Dulken et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2020; Zywitza et al., 2018) and in the septal wall which also harbours NSC niches (Mizrak et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the impact of scRNAseq technology on the field, supported by citations.

claim: The septal wall of the SVZ harbours NSC niches.
source: Since then, the single-cell RNA-sequencing has revolutionized the field and has made it possible to precisely elucidate the transcriptome of SVZ cells present in the LW (Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021; Dulken et al., 2017; Xie et al., 2020; Zywitza et al., 2018) and in the septal wall which also harbours NSC niches (Mizrak et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A FACS-based method using a combination of three surface markers (LeX, EGF receptor, CD24) allows sorting of five distinct SVZ cell populations: quiescent NSC, activated NSC, transit amplifying cells, immature neuroblasts, and migrating neuroblasts from the adult mouse brain.
source: We have previously developed a FACS-based method, using a combination of three surface markers (LeX, EGF receptor, CD24), allowing to sort five distinct SVZ cell populations: quiescent NSC (LeX-EGFR-CD24-, hereafter referred to as sorted-qNSC, s-qNSC), activated NSC (LeX +EGFR + CD24-, referred to as sorted, s-aNSC), transit amplifying cells (LeX-EGFR+CD24-, referred to as sorted, s-TAP), immature (LeX-EGFR+CD24low, referred to as sorted, s-iNB) and migrating neuroblasts (LeX-EGFR-CD24low, referred to as sorted, s-mNB) from the adult mouse brain (Daynac et al., 2015; Daynac et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a method previously developed by the authors, supported by citations to their own work.

claim: s-iNB presented neuroblast markers, for example CD24 and doublecortin (DCX).
source: Importantly, whereas s-iNB presented neuroblast markers, for example CD24 and doublecortin (DCX), s-iNB gathered the most abundant population among SVZ cycling progenitors (representing approximately 4.3% of total SVZ cells vs 1% s-aNSC and 2.5% s-TAP; Daynac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by previous data from the authors, cited in the text.

claim: s-iNB gathered the most abundant population among SVZ cycling progenitors, representing approximately 4.3% of total SVZ cells vs 1% s-aNSC and 2.5% s-TAP.
source: Importantly, whereas s-iNB presented neuroblast markers, for example CD24 and doublecortin (DCX), s-iNB gathered the most abundant population among SVZ cycling progenitors (representing approximately 4.3% of total SVZ cells vs 1% s-aNSC and 2.5% s-TAP; Daynac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is quantitative data from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Following a genotoxic stress (exposure to ionizing radiation) inducing the depletion of cycling progenitors, s-qNSC exit quiescence restoring successively s-aNSC, s-TAP, s-iNB and finally s-mNB.
source: We have previously shown that following a genotoxic stress (exposure to ionizing radiation) inducing the depletion of cycling progenitors, s-qNSC exit quiescence restoring successively s-aNSC, s-TAP, s-iNB and finally s-mNB (Daynac et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes findings from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Age-related SVZ neurogenesis decline is associated with TGFß signaling and specific cell cycle regulation changes in s-aNSC.
source: Transcriptomic studies revealed that age-related SVZ neurogenesis decline is associated with TGFß signaling and specific cell cycle regulation changes in s-aNSC.
evidence: This is based on transcriptomic studies, likely from the authors' previous work.

claim: A progressive lengthening of aNSC G1 phase with age leads to a decrease in the production of s-TAP, s-iNB, and s-mNB.
source: A progressive lengthening of aNSC G1 phase with age leads to a decrease in the production of s-TAP, s-iNB, and s-mNB (Daynac et al., 2013; Daynac et al., 2016; Pineda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including the authors' previous work.

claim: Despite the decrease of neurogenesis with aging, the s-iNB remained more abundant than s-aNSC and s-TAP in the aged brain.
source: However, despite the decrease of neurogenesis with aging the s-iNB remained more abundant than s-aNSC and s-TAP in the aged brain (Daynac et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: s-iNB had a clonogenic potential and were able to proliferate in vitro for weeks in normoxic conditions (20%O2) unlike s-mNB.
source: We have previously shown that s-iNB, which expressed the neuroblast markers CD24 and DCX (Daynac et al., 2013) and markers of neural progenitors such as Mash1 (Daynac et al., 2013), Dlx2 and SOX2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) had a clonogenic potential and were able to proliferate in vitro for weeks in normoxic conditions (20%O2) unlike s-mNB (Daynac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by previous data from the authors and data shown in the current manuscript.

claim: s-iNB exhibited reduced clonogenic potential compared to that of s-aNSC and s-TAP.
source: However, s-iNB exhibited reduced clonogenic potential compared to that of s-aNSC and s-TAP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hypoxic conditions (4%O2) promoted SVZ NSC proliferation and neurogenesis.
source: It has been previously reported that hypoxic conditions promoted SVZ NSC proliferation and neurogenesis (Li et al., 2021; Ross et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hypoxic conditions (4%O2) had no effects on s-mNB, but increased the proliferation capacities of s-aNSC, s-TAP and s-iNB, which reached similar growth rates.
source: Hypoxic conditions (4%O2) had no effects on s-mNB, but increased the proliferation capacities of s-aNSC, s-TAP and s-iNB, which reached similar growth rates, making them undistinguishable based on this endpoint (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hypoxic conditions increased the clonogenic potentials of both s-TAP and s-iNB but not that of s-aNSC.
source: Hypoxic conditions also increased the clonogenic potentials of both s-TAP and s-iNB but not that of s-aNSC (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In hypoxic conditions, the clonogenic potential of s-TAP reached similar values as s-aNSC, but that of s-iNB was still lower.
source: In these conditions, the clonogenic potential of s-TAP reached similar values as s-aNSC, but that of s-iNB was still lower (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Freshly isolated s-iNB had the capacity to generate the three neural lineages, neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, when plated for 5–7 days in the appropriate differentiation media, similarly as s-aNSC and s-TAP.
source: Quite surprisingly, freshly isolated s-iNB had the capacity to generate the three neural lineages, neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, when plated for 5–7 days in the appropriate differentiation media, similarly as s-aNSC and s-TAP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by differentiation assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Five weeks after transplantation, eGFP+ cells were detected in different regions of interest in the brains of mice transplanted with eGFP+s-NSC/TAP or eGFP+s-iNB, whereas no eGFP+ were observed after transplantation of eGFP+s-mNB even at the injection site.
source: Five weeks after transplantation, eGFP+ cells were detected in different regions of interest (Table 1) in the brains of mice transplanted with eGFP+s-NSC/TAP or eGFP+s-iNB, whereas no eGFP +were observed after transplantation of eGFP+s-mNB even at the injection site (IS) (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transplantation experiments with results shown in Table 1.

claim: Animals transplanted with eGFP+s-iNB presented high levels of eGFP+ cells in the OB with levels equivalent or superior to animals transplanted with eGFP+s-NSC/TAP, except in one out of three animals.
source: Excepted in one out of three, animals transplanted with eGFP+s-iNB presented high levels of eGFP+ cells in the OB with levels equivalent or superior to animals transplanted with eGFP+s-NSC/TAP or eGFP+s-iNB (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transplantation data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: EGFP+ cells were detected in the RMS as well as in the granular cell layer (GCL) and the external plexiform layer (EPL) of the OB where they differentiated into ΝeuN+ neurons in 2/3 animals transplanted with eGFP+s-iNB and in 3/3 animals transplanted with EGFP+s-NSC/TAP.
source: EGFP+ cells were detected in the RMS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) as well as in the granular cell layer (GCL) and the external plexiform layer (EPL) of the OB where they differentiated into ΝeuN+ neurons in 2/3 animals transplanted with eGFP+s-iNB (Figure 1Da) and in 3/3 animals transplanted with EGFP+s-NSC/TAP (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistological analysis shown in figures and Table 1.

claim: eGFP+ cells were present in the SVZ of all the animals transplanted with eGFP+s-iNB and eGFP+s-NSC/TAP, some of them expressing GFAP indicating the generation of astrocytes, and therefore possibly NSC.
source: Importantly, eGFP+ cells were present in the SVZ of all the animals transplanted with eGFP+s-iNB and eGFP+s-NSC/TAP (Figure 1Db, Figure 1Dc), some of them expressing GFAP indicating the generation of astrocytes, and therefore possibly NSC (Figure 1Db3, Figure 1Dc2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Plasticity of s-iNB was shown at the injection site by the detection of eGFP+ cells expressing markers of astrocytes (GFAP) and oligodendrocytes (CNPase).
source: Plasticity of s-iNB was also shown at the IS by the detection of eGFP+ cells expressing markers of astrocytes (GFAP) and oligodendrocytes (CNPase; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pseudotime analysis based on 3679 highly dispersed genes between the five sorted cell populations confirmed the lineage progression from s-qNSC (cluster1), then s-aNSC and s-TAP within a single cluster (cluster2), followed by s-iNB (cluster3) and finally s-mNB (cluster4).
source: Pseudotime analysis (TSCAN; Ji and Ji, 2016) based on 3679 highly dispersed genes between the five sorted cell populations confirmed the lineage progression from s-qNSC (cluster1), then s-aNSC and s-TAP within a single cluster (cluster2), followed by s-iNB (cluster3) and finally s-mNB (cluster4; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pseudotime analysis excluding s-qNSC, based on 1481 highly dispersed genes, delineated two distinct clusters for s-aNSC and s-TAP, highlighting their molecular differences.
source: Another pseudotime analysis excluding s-qNSC, based on 1481 highly dispersed genes, delineated two distinct clusters for s-aNSC and s-TAP (Figure 2C), highlighting their molecular differences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Venn diagram comparison of data sets revealed 2950, 315, 129, 395, and 1693 genes unique to s-qNSC, s-aNSC, s-TAP, s-iNB, and s-mNB respectively.
source: Venn diagram comparison of data sets revealed 2950, 315, 129, 395, and 1693 genes unique to s-qNSC, s-aNSC, s-TAP, s-iNB, and s-mNB respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of microarray data.

claim: S-aNSC overexpressed genes involved in metabolism of glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism.
source: S-aNSC overexpressed genes involved in metabolism of glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism.
evidence: This is based on functional profiling of transcriptomic data.

claim: S-qNSC rather overexpressed genes related to metabolism of lipids and Rho GTPase cycle.
source: S-qNSC rather overexpressed genes related to metabolism of lipids and Rho GTPase cycle.
evidence: This is based on functional profiling of transcriptomic data.

claim: S-TAP significantly displayed genes involved in Mitotic, G1 phase and G1/S transition, Activation of the pre-replicative complex.
source: S-TAP significantly displayed genes involved in Mitotic, G1 phase and G1/S transition, Activation of the pre-replicative complex.
evidence: This is based on functional profiling of transcriptomic data.

claim: S-mNB specifically overexpressed genes involved in axon guidance and nervous system development.
source: S-mNB specifically overexpressed genes involved in axon guidance and nervous system development.
evidence: This is based on functional profiling of transcriptomic data.

claim: s-iNB signatures contained many genes linked to cell cycle, prometaphase, M phase, and cell cycle checkpoints, clearly distinguishing them from the other cell populations including s-mNB.
source: Conversely, s-iNB signatures contained many genes linked to cell cycle, prometaphase, M phase, and cell cycle checkpoints, clearly distinguishing them from the other cell populations including s-mNB.
evidence: This is based on functional profiling of transcriptomic data.

claim: Alternative splicing (AS) plays various functions in brain development including neural cell differentiation and neuronal migration.
source: Alternative splicing (AS) plays various functions in brain development including neural cell differentiation and neuronal migration (Fisher and Feng, 2022; Grabowski, 2011; Jacko et al., 2018; Weyn-Vanhentenryck et al., 2018; Yano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: GO annotations of differentially spliced genes clearly revealed that spliced genes in SVZ cells are mainly involved in neuron development and neurogenesis.
source: GO annotations of DSG clearly revealed that spliced genes in SVZ cells are mainly involved in neuron development and neurogenesis.
evidence: This is based on analysis of differentially spliced genes from microarray data.

claim: qNSC differed from the other cell types by splicing concerning genes involved in mitosis and cell cycle, consistently with their quiescent state.
source: Interestingly, this also showed that qNSC logically differed from the other cell types by splicing concerning genes involved in mitosis and cell cycle, consistently with their quiescent state.
evidence: This is based on analysis of differentially spliced genes and is consistent with the known biology of quiescent cells.

claim: GO annotations of differentially spliced genes confirmed that s-TAP and s-iNB have distinct features.
source: More importantly, GO annotations of DSG confirmed that s-TAP and s-iNB have distinct features.
evidence: This is based on analysis of differentially spliced genes.

claim: There were 9484 differentially spliced genes between s-qNSC vs s-aNSC, no differentially spliced genes at the s-aNSC and s-TAP transition, only 169 between the s-TAP and s-iNB transition, and 3759 between s-iNB and s-mNB.
source: Results show a very large number of DSG between s-qNSC vs s-aNSC (9484) then no DSG at the s-aNSC and s-TAP transition, only 169 between the s-TAP and s-iNB transition, and finally 3759 between s-iNB and s-mNB (Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from analysis of differentially spliced genes.

claim: Functional profiling analysis linked the differentially spliced genes between s-TAP and s-iNB to the nervous system development and those between s-iNB vs s-mNB to protein binding or cell junction.
source: Functional profiling analysis with g:Profiler linked the DSG between s-TAP and s-iNB to the nervous system development and those between s-iNB vs s-mNB to protein binding or cell junction.
evidence: This is based on functional profiling analysis of differentially spliced genes.

claim: A clear down-regulation of most RNA splicing regulator (RSR) gene expression distinguishes s-qNSCs from the other populations.
source: Strikingly, a clear down-regulation of most RSR gene expression distinguishes s-qNSCs from the other populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression from microarray data.

claim: A shift in RSR gene expression discriminates s-aNSC and s-TAP from s-mNB.
source: Interestingly, another shift discriminates s-aNSC and s-TAP from s-mNB (Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression from microarray data.

claim: The switch in RSR expression between cycling progenitors and s-mNB occurred in s-iNB cells.
source: All these groups were up-regulated in s-iNB, suggesting that the switch in RSR expression between cycling progenitors and s-mNB occurred in these cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression patterns shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ptbp1, encoding a major splicing repressor, was downregulated in s-mNB as compared to s-iNB, consistently with the large increase in differentially spliced genes at the transition between s-iNB and s-mNB.
source: Interestingly, Ptbp1, encoding a major splicing repressor (Zhu et al., 2020), was downregulated in s-mNB as compared to s-iNB, consistently with the large increase in DSG at the transition between s-iNB and s-mNB.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Ptbp1 expression and its correlation with the number of differentially spliced genes.

claim: s-qNSC and s-mNB perfectly matched with the corresponding populations identified in published scRNAseq studies.
source: Violin plots show that s-qNSC and s-mNB perfectly matched with the corresponding populations identified in these studies, which was less obvious for s-aNSC and s-TAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on comparison of microarray data with published scRNAseq datasets.

claim: s-iNB matched with the clusters termed 'Mitosis' (Class VI) in the study of Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015 and 'Mitotic TAP' in that of Zywitza et al., 2018.
source: s-iNB matched with the clusters termed 'Mitosis' (Class VI) in the study of Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015 and 'Mitotic TAP' in that of Zywitza et al., 2018, and with clusters 8, 10, 17, 16 linked to 'Mitosis', but also with clusters 6 and 15 described as DCX+Ki67+ neuroblasts in the study by Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021.
evidence: This is based on comparison of microarray data with published scRNAseq datasets.

claim: s-iNB comprise cycling SVZ cells exhibiting both TAP and NB features, which illustrates the difficulties to determine the exact nature of cell clusters identified by scRNAseq.
source: These comparisons thus confirm that s-iNB comprise cycling SVZ cells exhibiting both TAP and NB features, which illustrates the difficulties to determine the exact nature of cell clusters identified by scRNAseq.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of sorted cell populations with scRNAseq clusters.

claim: After brain exposure to ionizing radiation, proliferating progenitors are highly radiation-sensitive and rapidly eliminated after irradiation.
source: We have previously reported (Daynac et al., 2013) that after brain exposure to ionizing radiation, proliferating progenitors are highly radiation-sensitive and rapidly eliminated after irradiation.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: qNSC that are radiation resistant repopulate the different SVZ neurogenic cell populations successively in the days following irradiation.
source: On the contrary qNSC that are radiation resistant repopulate the different SVZ neurogenic cell populations successively the following days after irradiation.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Based on a filtering criterion of 1500 genes/cell to exclude low-quality sequenced cells, 17,343 cells were retained for analysis, divided into 11,529 non-irradiated cells and 5814 irradiated cells.
source: Based on a filtering criterion of 1500 genes/cell to exclude low-quality sequenced cells, 17,343 cells were retained for analysis, divided into 11,529 non-irradiated cells and 5814 irradiated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the quality control and filtering of scRNAseq data.

claim: Leiden graph-based clustering, with a resolution of 1.2, identified 33 clusters.
source: Leiden graph-based clustering, with a resolution of 1.2, identified 33 clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the clustering analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: Nineteen clusters gathering more than half SVZ-residing cells corresponded to non-neurogenic cells.
source: Nineteen clusters gathering more than half SVZ-residing cells corresponded to non-neurogenic cells (ordered by decreasing abundance): microglia (expressing P2ry12 Gómez Morillas et al., 2021), ependymal cells (expressing both S100b and Slc1a3 Berger and Hediger, 1998), endothelial cells (expressing Flt1 Sawano et al., 2001), oligodendrocyte progenitors (OPC, expressing Pdgfra Zhu et al., 2014), Myelin forming oligodendrocytes (MFOL, expressing Mog Zywitza et al., 2018) and pericytes (expressing both Vtn and Pcam1 (Sohn et al., 2015; Lertkiatmongkol et al., 2016), and dopamine neurons (expressing Slc17a6 Kouwenhoven et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the identification of non-neurogenic cell clusters based on marker expression.

claim: The 14 other clusters corresponded to astrocytes and neurogenic cells.
source: The 14 other clusters corresponded to astrocytes and neurogenic cells (Figure 3B–C–D).
evidence: This describes the identification of neurogenic cell clusters.

claim: The clusters 4 and 13 that expressed S100b were further identified as qNSC (cluster 4) and astrocytes (cluster 13) based on the transcriptomic signatures described by Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021.
source: The clusters 4 and 13 that expressed S100b were further identified as qNSC (cluster 4) and astrocytes (cluster 13) based on the transcriptomic signatures described by Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the identification of specific clusters using published signatures.

claim: Cluster 17 was identified as aNSC based on Gfap, Thbs4, S100a6, Egfrlow and Ascl1 expressions.
source: Cluster 17, was identified as aNSC based on Gfap, Thbs4, S100a6, Egfrlow and Ascl1 expressions (Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021), and cluster 20 as TAP based on Egfr and Ascl1 expressions (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the identification of specific clusters based on marker expression and citations.

claim: Cluster 20 was identified as TAP based on Egfr and Ascl1 expressions.
source: Cluster 17, was identified as aNSC based on Gfap, Thbs4, S100a6, Egfrlow and Ascl1 expressions (Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021), and cluster 20 as TAP based on Egfr and Ascl1 expressions (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the identification of specific clusters based on marker expression and citations.

claim: Clusters 10, 5, 15, 12, and 8 were defined as cycling progenitors based on the expression of proliferative markers such as Top2a, Mki67, Ascl1.
source: Clusters 10, 5, 15, 12, and 8 were defined as cycling progenitors based on the expression of proliferative markers such as Top2a, Mki67, Ascl1.
evidence: This describes the identification of cycling progenitor clusters based on marker expression.

claim: Clusters 1, 3, 7, and 9 were identified as mNB due to the loss of Mki67, Top2a and Ascl1 expressions and the expression of Robo2 and Dcx.
source: Clusters 1, 3, 7, and 9 were identified as mNB due to the loss of Mki67, Top2 a and Ascl1 expressions and the expression of Robo2 and Dcx.
evidence: This describes the identification of mNB clusters based on marker expression.

claim: Cluster 19 did not express Ascl1 but expressed Top2a and Mki67 as well as Robo2 and Dcx, and was therefore positioned at the transition between iNB and mNB.
source: Cluster 19 did not expressed Ascl1 but Top2a and Mki67 as well as with Robo2 and Dcx, was therefore positioned at the transition between iNB and mNB.
evidence: This describes the identification and positioning of cluster 19 based on marker expression.

claim: UCell workflow allowed unequivocal attribution of some clusters to the sorted cell populations: cluster 4 and 13 matched with s-qNSC, cluster 17 with s-aNSC, cluster 20 with s-TAP, clusters 5, 15 and 12 with s-iNB and clusters 7, 9, 1 and 3 to s-mNB.
source: This score allowed us to unequivocally attribute some clusters to the sorted cell populations (Figure 3E, F and G): cluster 4 and 13 matched with s-qNSC, cluster 17 with s-aNSC, cluster 20 with s-TAP, clusters 5, 15 and 12 with s-iNB and finally clusters 7, 9, 1 and 3 to s-mNB.
evidence: This describes the results of UCell scoring analysis.

claim: The cluster 10 matched both with s-TAP and s-iNB and clusters 8 and 19 both to s-iNB and to s-mNB, reflecting the continuous nature of the SVZ neurogenic process.
source: Reflecting the continuous nature of the SVZ neurogenic process, the cluster 10 matched both with s-TAP and s-iNB and clusters 8 and 19 both to s-iNB and to s-mNB.
evidence: This describes the results of UCell scoring analysis and interprets them in the context of continuous differentiation.

claim: Cell-Cycle Scoring indicated that the clusters related to s-iNB were enriched in cells in S or G2/M phase.
source: Cell-Cycle Scoring (Zhu et al., 2014) indicated that the clusters related to s-iNB were enriched in cells in S or G/2 M phase (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on cell cycle scoring analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: The decreasing values of the recovery ratios evidence a temporal ordering of the regeneration of each cluster corresponding to s-iNB along with neurogenesis as follows: 10, 5, 15, 12, and 8.
source: The decreasing values of the ratios evidence a temporal ordering of the regeneration of each cluster corresponding to s-iNB along with neurogenesis as follows: 10, 5, 15, 12, and 8, the latter being the one at the iNB vs mNB transition as anticipated above.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cluster recovery after irradiation.

claim: The expression of RSR genes (Kdrbs3, Kdrbs1 Elavl3 and Elavl2, Elavl4, and Celf1) that were shown to increase along with neurogenesis in microarrays, also increased in cluster 10, remained stable in the other clusters related to s-iNB and reached a maximum value in the s-mNB clusters.
source: The expression of RSR genes (Kdrbs3, Kdrbs1 Elavl3 and Elavl2, Elavl4, and Celf1) that were shown to increase along with neurogenesis in microarrays, also increased in cluster 10, remained stable in the other clusters related to s-iNB and reached a maximum value in the s-mNB clusters (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression in scRNAseq clusters.

claim: The expressions of Mbnl1 and Msi2 that were shown to decrease along with neurogenesis in microarrays peaked in the clusters related to s-aNSC and s-TAP, decreased in the cluster 10, remained low in the clusters related to s-iNB and were not detected in the clusters related to s-mNB.
source: Conversely, the expressions of Mbnl1 and Msi2 that were shown to decrease along with neurogenesis in microarrays (Figure 4B) peaked in the clusters related to s-aNSC (Zywitza et al., 2018) and s-TAP (Daynac et al., 2013), decreased in the cluster 10, remained low in the clusters related to s-iNB (Gonzalez-Perez and Alvarez-Buylla, 2011; Dulken et al., 2017; Mich et al., 2014; Holmin et al., 1997) and were not detected in the clusters related to s-mNB (Daynac et al., 2015; Obernier and Alvarez-Buylla, 2019; Tong et al., 2015; Sohn et al., 2015; Nait-Oumesmar et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression in scRNAseq clusters.

claim: A major switch in the expression of RSR genes occurs in the clusters related to s-iNB.
source: Altogether, these data corroborate our microarray data and show that a major switch in the expression of RSR genes occurs in the clusters related to s-iNB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of RSR gene expression patterns.

claim: The splicing repressor Ptbp1 was similarly expressed in s-aNSC, s-TAP and s-iNB-related clusters but was downregulated progressively in the successive s-mNB clusters.
source: Interestingly, the splicing repressor Ptbp1 was similarly expressed in s-aNSC, s-TAP and s-iNB-related clusters but was downregulated progressively in the successive s-mNB clusters, suggesting that changes in Ptbp1 expression constitute an important molecular step for the final maturation of mNB, which involves a major increase of DSG.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Ptbp1 expression in scRNAseq clusters.

claim: Not all s-iNB were positive for doublecortin (Dcx) expression.
source: We have previously shown by immunofluorescence that not all the s-iNB were positive for doublecortin (Dcx) expression, a common marker of neuroblasts (Daynac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on previous immunofluorescence data from the authors.

claim: Dcx expression was restrained to s-mNB and to clusters related to s-iNB in which it increased consistently with their hierarchical ordering.
source: Violin plot (Figure 3D) and feature plot (Figure 5A) show that Dcx expression was restrained to s-mNB and to clusters related to s-iNB in which it increased consistently with their hierarchical ordering we defined above.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Dcx expression in scRNAseq data.

claim: The ratios of numbers of cells per cluster indicated a greater recovery of Dcxlow cells as compared to Dcxhigh cells in s-iNB-related clusters from irradiated brains, reflecting their temporal ordering.
source: The ratios of numbers of cells per cluster indicated a greater recovery of Dcxlow cells as compared to Dcxhigh cells in s-iNB-related clusters from irradiated brains (Figure 5B), reflecting their temporal ordering.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cell recovery after irradiation.

claim: Characterization of differentially expressed genes according to the Dcx status in iNB clusters showed 588 unique genes expressed in the Dcxlow cells and 98 genes specifically expressed in the Dcxhigh cells.
source: Characterization of differentially expressed genes according to the Dcx status in these clusters showed 588 unique genes expressed in the Dcxlow cells and 98 genes specifically expressed in the Dcxhigh cells.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Genes related to metabolism of RNA were overrepresented in the Dcxlow cells, whereas genes linked to GABAergic synapse, neuronal system were rather overexpressed in the Dcxhigh cells.
source: Functional enrichment profiling using the g:Profiler software illustrates biological differences between both populations: genes related to metabolism of RNA were overrepresented in the Dcxlow cells, whereas genes linked to GABAergic synapse, neuronal system were rather overexpressed in the Dcxhigh cells (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on functional enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: 55% of Dcxhigh cell specific genes were s-mNB genes (e.g. Robo2, Gap43, Nav3).
source: Notably, 55% of Dcxhigh cell specific genes were s-mNB genes (e.g. Robo2, Gap43, Nav3).
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene lists.

claim: Progressive transcriptomic changes occurred between Dcxlow and Dcxhigh cells in iNB clusters.
source: Further analysis of RSR genes expression in function of the Dcx status, clearly confirms that progressive transcriptomic changes occurred between Dcxlow and Dcxhigh cells (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression in Dcxlow and Dcxhigh cells.

claim: RSR gene profiles of Dcxlow cells in clusters related to s-iNB were different from that related to both s-TAP and s-NSC, and that of Dcxhigh cells from that of s-mNB.
source: However, RSR gene profiles of Dcxlow cells in clusters related to s-iNB were obviously different from that related to both s-TAP and s-NSC, and that of Dcxhigh cells from that of s-mNB.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression patterns.

claim: The clusters related to s-iNB contained cells engaged in neuronal differentiation that are molecularly distinct from the other types of SVZ neurogenic cells already characterized.
source: These data clearly show that the clusters related to s-iNB contained cells engaged in neuronal differentiation that are molecularly distinct from the other types of SVZ neurogenic cells already characterized This suggest that s-iNB correspond to a new stage of cycling neurogenic progenitors progressively engaged in neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular characterization of iNB clusters.

claim: s-iNB correspond to a new stage of cycling neurogenic progenitors progressively engaged in neuronal differentiation.
source: These data clearly show that the clusters related to s-iNB contained cells engaged in neuronal differentiation that are molecularly distinct from the other types of SVZ neurogenic cells already characterized This suggest that s-iNB correspond to a new stage of cycling neurogenic progenitors progressively engaged in neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular and functional characterization of iNB cells.

claim: Recombinant eGFP+ iNB exhibited a clonogenic potential and a rate of population doublings quite similar to eGFP- iNB and total iNB, contrary to eGFP+ mNB, which did not show clonogenic potential and did not proliferate at long-term in vitro.
source: As shown in Figure 6A and B, recombinant eGFP+ iNB exhibited a clonogenic potential and a rate of population doublings quite similar to eGFP- iNB and total iNB, contrary to eGFP+ mNB, which did not show clonogenic potential and did not proliferate at long-term in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by clonogenicity and proliferation assays shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Both eGFP+ iNB and eGFP- iNB have the capacity to generate the three neural lineages, neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, when plated for 5–7 day in the appropriate differentiation media.
source: Moreover, we showed that both eGFP+ iNB and eGFP- iNB have the capacity to generate the three neural lineages, neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, when plated for 5–7 day in the appropriate differentiation media (Figure 6C), similarly as s-iNB (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by differentiation assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When eGFP+iNB were transplanted into the brain of C57Bl/6 J mice, no eGFP+ cells persisted at long-term (5 weeks).
source: By contrast, when eGFP+iNB were transplanted into the brain of C57Bl/6 J mice, no eGFP+ cells persisted at long-term (5 weeks; Table 2), suggesting that the in vivo plasticity and regenerative properties of s-iNB was rather associated to Dcxlow iNB.
evidence: This is demonstrated by transplantation experiments with results shown in Table 2.

claim: The in vivo plasticity and regenerative properties of s-iNB was rather associated to Dcxlow iNB.
source: By contrast, when eGFP+iNB were transplanted into the brain of C57Bl/6 J mice, no eGFP+ cells persisted at long-term (5 weeks; Table 2), suggesting that the in vivo plasticity and regenerative properties of s-iNB was rather associated to Dcxlow iNB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transplantation results showing that Dcxhigh (eGFP+) iNB did not persist.

claim: Previous studies of SVZ neural progenitors have been essentially focused on the characterization of the molecular mechanisms regulating quiescence, activation and the regenerative potential of aNSC.
source: Studies of SVZ neural progenitors have been essentially focused on the characterization of the molecular mechanisms regulating quiescence, activation and the regenerative potential of aNSC.
evidence: This is a statement about the focus of previous research in the field.

claim: iNB is an abundant population of cycling progenitors, which is more advanced towards neuronal differentiation than TAP, while retaining unexpected stem cell properties unlike mNB.
source: We show that iNB is an abundant population of cycling progenitors, which is more advanced towards neuronal differentiation than TAP, while retaining unexpected stem cell properties unlike mNB.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Major splicing regulations in iNB might be critical for the final commitment to the neuronal fate.
source: We suggest that major splicing regulations in iNB might be critical for the final commitment to the neuronal fate.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed changes in splicing regulators.

claim: Neural progenitors in previous studies have been gathered in either 'mitotic' clusters or 'neural progenitor cells' clusters that lacked clear biological significance and prevented the identification of subtypes of SVZ cycling progenitors.
source: Indeed, neural progenitors in these studies cycling have been gathered in either 'mitotic' clusters (Cebrian-Silla et al., 2021; Zywitza et al., 2018; Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015) or 'neural progenitor cells' clusters (Dulken et al., 2017) that lacked clear biological significance and prevented the identification of subtypes of SVZ cycling progenitors.
evidence: This is a critique of previous scRNAseq studies based on the authors' analysis.

claim: The study, combining for the first time characterization of FAC-sorted cells and an irradiation-based model of sequential regeneration, clearly distinguished the molecular profiles of TAP and iNB among cycling progenitors reflecting differences in their respective potentials in vitro and in vivo.
source: Our study, combining for the first time characterization of FAC-sorted cells and an irradiation-based model of sequential regeneration, clearly distinguished the molecular profiles of TAP and iNB among cycling progenitors reflecting differences in their respective potentials in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological approach and findings of the study.

claim: The results constitute a valuable resource for delineating the molecular transitions occurring during neurogenesis that are orchestrated by numerous differentially expressed genes and alternative splicing variants.
source: Our results constitute thus a valuable resource for delineating the molecular transitions occurring during neurogenesis that are orchestrated by numerous differentially expressed genes and alternative splicing variants.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the study's findings.

claim: The transition from qNSC to aNSC has been abundantly investigated in the literature, but the transcriptional shift leading to the differentiation of neural progenitors into neuroblasts has not been thoroughly analyzed to date.
source: The transition from qNSC to aNSC has been abundantly investigated in the literature (Dulken et al., 2017; Llorens-Bobadilla et al., 2015), but the transcriptional shift leading to the differentiation of neural progenitors into neuroblasts has not been thoroughly analyszed to date.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in previous research.

claim: The transcriptional shift leading to the differentiation of neural progenitors into neuroblasts occurs in immature neuroblasts.
source: We showed that it occurs in immature neuroblasts, which form a relatively abundant subpopulation of SVZ cells, which exhibit specific transcriptional features distinguishing them from TAP and mNB.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: A subset of neuroblasts co-expressing Ascl1 and Dcx or CD24low expressing low levels of EGFR in the adult SVZ has been described previously.
source: This was consistent with prior findings describing a subset of neuroblasts co-expressing Ascl1 and Dcx or CD24low expressing low levels of EGFR in the adult SVZ (Pastrana et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Ponti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: s-iNB comprise a molecularly distinct population of cycling cells at the transition between TAP and mNB, and exhibiting molecular characteristics of both these cell types.
source: Here, we evidenced that s-iNB comprise a molecularly distinct population of cycling cells at the transition between TAP and mNB, and exhibiting molecular characteristics of both these cell types.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The capacity of neuroblasts to reorient towards the glial lineage in pathological contexts have been reported previously.
source: The capacity of neuroblasts to reorient towards the glial lineage in pathological contexts have been reported previously (El Waly et al., 2018; Jablonska et al., 2010; Klein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: s-iNB kept in vitro and in vivo a regenerative potential similar to that of s-aNSC and s-TAP.
source: Consistent with the molecular findings showing that s-iNB kept transcriptional features of NSC and TAP, we showed that s-iNB also kept in vitro and in vivo a regenerative potential similar to that of s-aNSC and s-TAP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the differentiation and transplantation experiments.

claim: The detection of GFAP-positive engrafted cells persisting in the SVZ suggests that s-iNB may have the capacity to dedifferentiate in vivo and generate NSC.
source: Importantly, this may also include the capacity to dedifferentiate in vivo and generate NSC as suggested by the detection of GFAP-positive engrafted cells persisting in the SVZ.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the detection of GFAP+ cells in the SVZ after transplantation.

claim: s-iNB corresponded to several scRNAseq clusters, which were not clearly characterized in the literature.
source: Interestingly, s-iNB corresponded to several scRNAseq clusters, which were not clearly characterized in the literature.
evidence: This is based on comparison of sorted cell populations with published scRNAseq data.

claim: The model of SVZ regeneration established the hierarchical ordering of iNB-related clusters, in which progressive molecular changes leading to the differentiation into migrating neuroblasts were shown.
source: Our model of SVZ regeneration established the hierarchical ordering of these clusters, in which we showed progressive molecular changes leading to the differentiation into migrating neuroblasts.
evidence: This is based on the irradiation model and analysis of cluster recovery.

claim: Dcxhigh cells in iNB clusters have transcriptional features confirming they are more engaged in the differentiation than their Dcxlow counterparts.
source: Dcxhigh cells in these clusters have transcriptional features confirming they are more engaged in the differentiation than their Dcxlow counterparts.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis between Dcxlow and Dcxhigh cells.

claim: Dcxhigh and Dcxlow cells in iNB clusters remained molecularly distinct from both TAP and mNB.
source: Importantly, we showed that Dcxhigh and Dcxlow cells in these clusters remained molecularly distinct from both TAP and mNB.
evidence: This is based on molecular profiling of these cell populations.

claim: iNB cells can be divided into two subclasses: iNB1 cells, corresponding to Dcxlow iNB, immediately succeeding the TAP and iNB2 cells, corresponding to Dcxhigh iNB and preceding the stage mNB.
source: We thus propose a revision of the current model of SVZ neurogenesis by introducing iNB cells, as highly cycling progenitors that undergo progressive neuronal differentiation but kept multipotency (Figure 7). iNB cells could be further divided in two subclasses of cells depending on their progression into the neuronal differentiation process: iNB1 cells, corresponding to Dcxlow iNB, immediately succeeding the TAP and iNB2 cells, corresponding to Dcxhigh iNB and preceding the stage mNB.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Both iNB1 and iNB2 cells kept transcriptomic features that differentiated them from both TAP and mNB.
source: Importantly, we showed that both iNB1 and iNB2 cells kept transcriptomic features that differentiated them from both TAP and mNB, whereas iNB1 cells kept a regenerative potential both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is based on molecular profiling and functional assays.

claim: iNB1 cells kept a regenerative potential both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Importantly, we showed that both iNB1 and iNB2 cells kept transcriptomic features that differentiated them from both TAP and mNB, whereas iNB1 cells kept a regenerative potential both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is based on functional assays showing that Dcxlow (iNB1) cells have regenerative properties.

claim: AS events are known to play important roles in neural cell differentiation, neuronal migration, synapse formation, and brain development.
source: AS events are known to play important roles in neural cell differentiation, neuronal migration, synapse formation, and brain development (Grabowski, 2011; Yano et al., 2010; Mauger et al., 2015; Shin and Kim, 2013; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neurons are characterized by a pervasive use of alternative exons.
source: Neurons are characterized by a pervasive use of alternative exons (Irimia et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There was a dramatic increase in differentially spliced genes at the transition between s-iNB and s-mNB.
source: Consistently, we showed a dramatic increase in DSG at the transition between s-iNB and s-mNB.
evidence: This is based on analysis of differentially spliced genes from microarray data.

claim: These alternative splicing events are clearly related to major changes in RNA splicing regulators (RSR) expressions occurring in s-iNB.
source: These alternative splicing events are clearly related to major changes in RNA splicing regulators (RSR) expressions occurring in s-iNB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between RSR expression changes and increased alternative splicing.

claim: Some RSR genes upregulated in s-aNSC, s-TAP, such as Msi1 and Msi2, have a known role in maintenance and renewal of stem cells.
source: Consistently, some genes upregulated in s-aNSC, s-TAP, such as Msi1 and Msi2, have a known role in maintenance and renewal of stem cells (Fox et al., 2015; Sakakibara and Okano, 1997; Yano et al., 2016), while some others upregulated in s-mNB, such as Elavl3 and 4, have known roles in many neuronal processes (Yano et al., 2016; Bronicki and Jasmin, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Some RSR genes upregulated in s-mNB, such as Elavl3 and 4, have known roles in many neuronal processes.
source: Consistently, some genes upregulated in s-aNSC, s-TAP, such as Msi1 and Msi2, have a known role in maintenance and renewal of stem cells (Fox et al., 2015; Sakakibara and Okano, 1997; Yano et al., 2016), while some others upregulated in s-mNB, such as Elavl3 and 4, have known roles in many neuronal processes (Yano et al., 2016; Bronicki and Jasmin, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Genes of both groups of RSR genes were overexpressed in scRNAseq clusters related to s-iNB, which undoubtedly distinguished these cells from both s-TAP and s-mNB.
source: Interestingly, genes of both groups of genes were overexpressed in scRNAseq clusters related to s-iNB, which thus undoubtedly distinguished these cells from both s-TAP and s-mNB and confirmed that important molecular switches for neuronal differentiation occurred in D cells.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression in scRNAseq clusters.

claim: Important molecular switches for neuronal differentiation occurred in iNB cells.
source: Interestingly, genes of both groups of genes were overexpressed in scRNAseq clusters related to s-iNB, which thus undoubtedly distinguished these cells from both s-TAP and s-mNB and confirmed that important molecular switches for neuronal differentiation occurred in D cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in RSR gene expression.

claim: The transcriptomic switches in RSR genes occurred sequentially from iNB1 cells to iNB2 cells.
source: Further analysis of scRNAseq clusters showed that these transcriptomic switches occurred sequentially from iNB1 cells to iNB2 cells.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RSR gene expression in Dcxlow and Dcxhigh cells.

claim: The expression of Elavl4 progressively increased from the Dcxlow iNB1 cells to the Dcxhigh iNB2 cells fractions, confirming their progressive commitment into neuroblasts.
source: Indeed, the expression of Elavl4 progressively increased from the Dcxlow iNB1 cells to the Dcxhigh iNB2 cells fractions, confirming their progressive commitment into neuroblasts, and overall, the interest of discriminating these two cell types in the model of SVZ neurogenesis we propose (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of Elavl4 expression in Dcxlow and Dcxhigh cells.

claim: Expression of Ptbp1 may play an important role in maintaining the regenerative properties in iNB1 cells.
source: Strikingly, the splicing repressor, Ptbp1, was expressed in iNB1 cells at levels similar to those in s-aNSC and s-TAP, but decreased in iNB2 cells, and was undetectable in migrating neuroblasts. This suggests that expression of Ptbp1 may play an important role in maintaining the regenerative properties in iNB1 cells, which should be further investigated.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the correlation between Ptbp1 expression and regenerative properties.

claim: The study has been performed on cells collected from the SVZ the lateral walls of the ventricles of young adult mice.
source: Our study has been performed on cells collected from the SVZ the LWs of the ventricles of young adult mice.
evidence: This describes the source of cells used in the study.

claim: The transcriptional signatures provided may be useful for further characterization of neurogenic cells present in the septal wall of the SVZ.
source: The transcriptional signatures we provide here may thus be useful for further characterization of neurogenic cells present in the septal wall of the SVZ (Mizrak et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of the study's findings.

claim: iNB cells are a relatively abundant population in the adult SVZ that kept unexpected plasticity and multipotency that persist in the aged brain.
source: To conclude, we have characterized the molecular features of iNB cells, a relatively abundant population in the adult SVZ that kept unexpected plasticity and multipotency that persist in the aged brain (Daynac et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings with a citation to previous work.

claim: iNB cells may represent a new target in regenerative medicine.
source: They may thus represent a new target in regenerative medicine.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential therapeutic relevance of iNB cells.

claim: iNB cells undergo major transcriptomic changes involving AS and associated to switches in RSR genes expression.
source: We have shown that these cells undergo major transcriptomic changes involving AS and associated to switches in RSR genes expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Dysregulations of many RSR genes have been involved in cancer and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Dysregulations of many of these RSR genes have been involved in cancer and neurodegenerative diseases (Kang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Further characterization of iNB cells using the tools developed may be useful to determine the potential therapeutic targeting of these cells in various brain pathologies.
source: Further characterization of iNB cells using the tools we developed may be useful to determine the potential therapeutic targeting of these cells in various brain pathologies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.
